10417-love-life-work-being-a-book-of-opi:
Elbert Hubbard published this book of opinions in 1906, promising good-natured advice on how to find happiness with the least harm to others. Hubbard, founder of the Roycroft arts community, writes in short, aphoristic chapters that mix cheer, scolding, and common sense. The book is a miscellany, not a system.

Chapters treat prayer, time and chance, religious revivals, mental attitude, outsiders, art, progress, sympathy, and work versus waste. Hubbard urges initiative, honesty, and kind action over worry about the future. Readers get a brisk, early self-help book, full of maxims on love, life, and work.
10485-experiments-in-government-and-the-:
Elihu Root published this constitutional study in 1913, on experiments in government and the essentials of the American Constitution. Root, a statesman and lawyer, sees two assaults at work: socialism against individualism, and reform against institutions said to fail the social order. He defends liberty and private property as foundations.

Root shows how America changed since 1787, when slow travel kept states apart, to a time when production and trade ignore state lines. Institutions, he argues, must grow with that new life. Readers get a clear, conservative case for constitutional adaptation without abandoning its core.
12296-camps-and-trails-in-china-a-narrat:
Roy Chapman Andrews published Camps and Trails in China as a narrative of exploration, adventure, and sport in little-known China. Andrews, associate curator of mammals at the American Museum of Natural History, led the museum Asiatic Zoological Expedition of 1916 to 1917.

The book opens with a camp on a snow mountain at twelve thousand feet. It then follows caravans along gorges where sides fall hundreds of feet to green torrents. Those torrents rush toward the sea two thousand five hundred miles away. Andrews describes hunting, mapping, and collecting specimens among peoples and places few Westerners had seen. The narrative mixes science with adventure. It shows early twentieth-century exploration at its most confident and curious.
16368-the-white-ladies-of-worcester-a-ro:
Florence L. Barclay's White Ladies of Worcester, published by Putnam in 1917, is a romance of the twelfth century set among nuns. Contents move through a subterranean way, Sister Mary Antony discoursing, the prioress passing, a plea for tenderness, a wayward nun, and a knight of the bloody vest. The Madonna in the cloister, wings of the storm, and the prioress shutting the door deepen the tale.

Later chapters bring a confession of recognition, years rolling back, a farewell here and now, echoes of wild voices, the cathedral crypt, and holly and mistletoe. Barclay, author of The Rosary, writes devout, emotional romance. Readers who like medieval convents, knights, and faithful hearts will find a tender, atmospheric novel.
16700-the-ancient-church-its-history-doc:
W. D. Killen, professor of church history in Ireland, traces the ancient church for its first three hundred years in this 1859 New York edition, corrected by his own hand. Period one runs from Christ's birth to John's death in AD 100. It opens with Rome's empire at Christ's birth: its bounds, strength, orators, poets, and moral state, with Epicureans, Stoics, and current polytheism.

Killen writes as a Presbyterian scholar, careful with sources and fair in tone. The book suits students of early Christianity who want history, doctrine, worship, and constitution together. It remains a solid Victorian survey of the church's first centuries.
18971-jacobean-embroidery-its-forms-and-:
Ada Wentworth Fitzwilliam and A. F. Morris Hands wrote this illustrated study of Jacobean embroidery, published in London in 1912 by Kegan Paul, Trench, Trübner. It covers late Tudor work and early seventeenth-century designs, with sections on blue crewel work and other forms and fillings. Several plates had first appeared in Needlecraft Monthly Magazine.

The book gives makers both history and practice: an introductory history by Hands, then detailed accounts of patterns, stitches, and motifs. Readers interested in needlework get a careful guide to a rich period of English embroidery, with plates to study. It also serves historians of domestic craft, showing what skilled hands made for homes of the period.
20363-continental-monthly-vol-5-no-6-jun:
The Continental Monthly for June 1864, volume five, number six, covers literature and art. One essay calls a certain religion the most wonderful thing in history. It starts in an obscure corner of an obscure province, it notes. Its founder dies as a felon among felons on a cross.

Its teachers are peasants fettered by a narrow dialect of an unknown tongue. Yet that faith remade the world, the essay marvels in awe. The Monthly served Union readers with essays amid the Civil War. This issue shows its mix of faith, letters, and wartime thought.
20481-continental-monthly-vol-6-no-1-jul:
The Continental Monthly called itself a magazine devoted to literature and national policy. This is its July 1864 issue, volume 6, number 1. It appeared while the Civil War still raged, and its essays weigh the nation's past and future.

One article describes an American institution as built without any regular plan. It grew, the writer says, by gradual additions and by copying European features, from the Revolution to the present. Even so, it has worked with great vigor and effect. The issue shows Northern readers arguing over what the war was making of their country.
20509-daring-and-suffering-a-history-of-:
William Pittenger's Daring and Suffering tells the true story of the Great Locomotive Chase of 1862. Pittenger was one of the Union soldiers who stole a Confederate train in Georgia. Their roll of honor lists men of the Twenty-first and Thirty-third Ohio Volunteers.

The raiders meant to burn bridges and cut the railroad behind enemy lines. Captured, some were hanged as spies, while others escaped or were exchanged. Pittenger wrote from his own suffering in Confederate prisons. His book became the classic account of the raid, and its men received the first Medals of Honor.
24726-a-history-of-art-for-beginners-and:
Clara Erskine Clement wrote this survey for students, covering painting, sculpture, and building design from ancient times to her own day. Copyrighted in 1887, it moves from Egypt, Assyria, and Greece through medieval church art to the painting schools of Italy, Flanders, Spain, France, and England. Short lives of noted artists run through the chapters.

Clement keeps her language plain and points the reader to pictures and carvings that show each style at its best. A chapter on Titian, for instance, follows him from Venice to the courts of emperors and popes. For a new student, the book still works as a clear road map through the main schools and masters of Western art.
25632-a-history-of-art-for-beginners-and:
Clara Erskine Clement writes this history of art for beginners and students, covering painting, sculpture, and architecture, with complete indexes and numerous pictures, published in New York by Frederick A. Stokes in 1891 with a 1887 copyright. The Venus of Milo fronts the book.

Chapters treat ancient sculpture in Egypt and Assyria, Greek sculpture, ancient Italian sculpture, and medieval sculpture from the fifth to the fifteenth century. Italian sculpture in the fifteenth century follows, with sculpture in Germany, France, England, and other lands, giving students a clear survey in order. Clement also wrote a handbook of legendary and mythological art.
30710-the-origins-and-destiny-of-imperia:
J. A. Cramb, late professor of modern history at Queen's College, London, wrote this study of imperial Britain in nineteenth-century Europe, published by John Murray in 1915. A biographical note and portrait of the author open the volume. Cramb asks how Britain's empire grew, what forces shaped it, and where its destiny might lead in a Europe of rival powers.

The book looks back to Rome as a model of empire, and forward to Britain's place among modern states, weighing war, trade, sea power, and national character. Its tone is that of a lecture hall in wartime, confident about Britain's mission and troubled by its costs. Historians will find a frank statement of Edwardian imperial thought, best read now as both history and a record of its own age.
31774-si-klegg-book-4-experiences-of-si-:
John McElroy's fourth Si Klegg book, in its second edition of 1910, follows Si Klegg and Shorty through the Great Tullahoma Campaign. On June 23, 1863, after six months around Murfreesboro, the Army of the Cumberland's 60,000 men swept forward in nine days of drenching rain and drove Bragg from his strong positions.

Twenty chapters carry the pair from Duck River and balky mules to the advance on Tullahoma, a Fourth of July celebration, love letters, mountain folk, hospital days, and a tedious convalescence. Readers get a Civil War campaign story that mixes hard marching and battle with the small humors of camp life.
32749-the-challenge-of-the-country-a-stu:
George Walter Fiske Jr., junior dean of Oberlin Theological Seminary, challenges college men and women to invest their talents in rural life, in this Association Press volume of 1912. He dedicates the book to those who cherish rural life enough to withstand the city's pull.

Eight chapters treat the rural problem, country life optimism, the new rural civilization, and the triumphs of scientific agriculture. Fiske cites a hardy wild peach from Northern China and a wild wheat from Palestine, tested for American farms. Later chapters weigh cooperation, rural education, the community-serving church, and the leadership the countryside needs.
34030-turning-and-boring-a-specialized-t:
Franklin D. Jones, associate editor of Machinery, wrote this specialized treatise on turning and boring, first copyrighted in 1914 and in a fifth printing in 1919. It serves machinists, students in industrial and engineering schools, and apprentices, covering modern practice with engine lathes, turret lathes, and vertical and horizontal boring machines.

Early chapters explain the engine lathe in full: cylindrical turning, facing, roughing and finishing cuts, centers, arbors, and rests. Jones writes in clear shop language with working detail. The book still serves readers who want the lathe crafts of its age.
7274-poets-of-the-south-a-series-of-biog:
F. V. N. Painter, professor of modern languages at Roanoke College, presents the poets of the South in biographical and critical studies with typical poems, annotated. His preface argues that these singers form a worthy galaxy of talent, yet remain little read even in the South, which might be expected to take pride in them. An age of prose and practical interests, he says, has drifted readers away from poetry.

Painter answers that drift with lives and poems side by side, so that a reader can meet each poet and judge the verse at once. The studies mix fact with criticism, favouring clear judgment over praise. The book serves as an introduction to a regional tradition too often passed over.
britannica-1911-batu:
Batu, or Rock Islands, called Batoe in Dutch, is a group of islands in the Dutch East Indies, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The group holds three larger islands and forty-eight smaller ones, west of Sumatra. The strait of Sibirut splits it from the Mentawi group. The three chief islands, from north to south, are Pini or Mintao, Masa, and Bala. The land comes to 445 square miles.

Land and people close the account. The islands are in general low and covered with forest, in which the coconut palm stands out. Trade is carried on in coconuts, coconut oil, and other produce of the woods. The native people number about 3000. They are of Malayan or older stock, akin to the people of the island of Nias to the north-west. Only about twenty of the smaller islands are lived on.
camps-and-trails-in-china-a-narrative-of:
Roy Chapman Andrews and Yvette Borup Andrews wrote a tale of hunt and search in far China, printed in 1918. Roy led the American Museum's Asia beast hunt of 1916-1917. Yvette shot the trip's photos. Appleton of New York and London put out the book. Henry Fairfield Osborn, the museum's head, gets it in thanks.

A camp on Snow Mountain at 12,000 feet fronts the plates. Little-known China is the ground the title vows. Beast hunts, trail camps, and sport fill the run, by the sub-title's word. Roy's past whale book heads his name. Verse at the front calls to probe the still spots and take what luck gives. Museum science and wild sport ride side by side through the whole.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cesare-cantu:
Cesare Cantù was an Italian historian and poet born at Brivio on 8 December 1807 and dying at Milan on 11 March 1895. He first studied theology but left the seminary without finishing, not feeling called to the priesthood. Turning to literature, he taught Italian language and literature, first at Sondrio in 1823, then at Como in 1827, and finally at Milan in 1832.

At Como he wrote the verse tale Algiso. His history of the city and diocese of Como made him better known. His Ragionamenti on seventeenth-century Lombard history expressed liberal views on Austrian policy. They earned him thirteen months' imprisonment, whose miseries he described in the novel Margherita Pusterla. About then he began his greatest work, the Storia universale in 35 volumes, reprinted often and translated into English, German, French, and Spanish.
doe-osti-17134351-south-asia-group-for-e:
Sarah Turner of the National Laboratory of the Rockies leads session 1 of a virtual training on Engage, dated September 2026, for the South Asia Group for Energy. SAGE backs secure, affordable, and modern energy systems across South Asia through technical cooperation. The training series teaches energy modeling tools for resource assessment, siting, and planning.

Engage is an open access web tool for capacity expansion and operations modeling, hosted by the laboratory. It can optimize electricity, fuel, water, and transport systems together, at scales from a district to a continent. Slides pose the questions it answers, from the role of nuclear or geothermal power to the cheapest path to 2050 targets. Session steps cover gathering asset cost and performance data and time series resource data.
doe-osti-3001268-let-s-stick-together-in:
Tanner Finney, Rian Nguy, Abigail Wilson and seven Los Alamos colleagues ask why corn stover jams biorefineries in LA-UR-25-27223, issued 3 November 2025. Stalks, leaves and cobs milled into crumbles should flow like grain; instead they bridge, clog and stop lines. Sorting the plant into anatomical fractions before milling is one proposed fix. The team tested whether fraction, moisture or particle size really governs the flow.

Shear cells, friction measurements, gas chromatography of surface energy, vapour sorption and microscopy covered the bases. Moisture dominated everything: wetter stover gained unconfined yield strength and lost flow function across every fraction. Surface energy differed between fractions without moving bulk behaviour. Coarse 6-millimetre particles flowed worse than 4-millimetre ones, blamed on wider size spread and interlocking. The practical verdict: skip the fractionation expense, control moisture and size distribution instead. Unfractionated stover, kept dry, handles just as well.
doe-osti-3005457-multiple-hypothesis-tra:
Jennifer Jean Sanderson writes a course project paper, SAND2025-14606R, for a graduate electrical engineering class, ECE 8851. The topic is navigation by other people's signals. Low Earth orbit communication satellites flood the sky with radio transmissions never meant for navigation. Receivers can still extract timing from them, if they can tell which satellite sent which signal.

Sanderson applies multiple hypothesis tracking to that identification problem: keeping several candidate assignments alive until the evidence separates them. Public two-line element sets plus an orbit propagator supply rough satellite positions. The work builds on her earlier nearest-neighbor data association study with Kassas, presented in 2025. Megaconstellation navigation is attractive because it works where GPS is jammed or spoofed, a growing concern the paper speaks to directly.
doe-osti-3010913-effects-of-dose-rate-on:
Dose rate changes the damage that ion beams leave in gamma lithium aluminate pellets, according to PNNL-38365 by Jiang, Casella, and Senor of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. Experiments ran from November 2024 to September 2025 using sequential irradiation with 120 keV helium ions and 80 keV D2 ions. Three dose rates, 7.3, 2.9, and 0.68 in units of 10^-4 dpa per second, each delivered the same total fluence of 2 x 10^17 ions per square centimetre at 500 degrees C.

The peak combined dose reached 7.55 dpa near 255 nanometres depth. Medium and high dose rates produced an amorphous surface layer, a crystalline layer holding LiAl5O8 precipitates, and blisters at their interface. The low dose rate sample stayed crystalline with cavities instead, characterised by STEM and ToF-SIMS.
doe-osti-3015855-performance-evaluation-:
C J Taylor Mason, Subhashish Meher, James Fitzpatrick, and seven Pacific Northwest National Laboratory colleagues wrote report M3CT-25PN1307041 in September 2025. They evaluated parts made from 316H stainless steel by laser powder bed fusion, a printing process that fuses thin powder layers with a laser. The parts are candidates for use in advanced nuclear reactors.

Testing combined ultrasound, X-ray diffraction, and X-ray tomography, which found density above 99 percent and mapped leftover stresses from about minus 47.6 to plus 19.2 megapascals. Flow-3D simulations with machine learning corrections predicted porosity with under 1 percent error. Smarter support structures cut one build from 349 hours to 142 hours. An elbow pipe printed at 40 percent scale showed that complex shapes are feasible for microreactor designs.
doe-osti-3024597-bil-high-speed-fuel-cel:
Tom Bronchetti of General Motors LLC filed this final report on March 26, 2026, for award DE-EE0011340, the BIL High Speed Fuel Cell Stack Manufacturing project. The grant period was set to run from October 2024 to June 2027, but the project was terminated on December 31, 2025, inside its first budget period. This short report closes the award out and states plainly what was and was not done.

The objective had been to design, build, and deploy a line able to produce 20,000 next-generation fuel cell stacks per year. Planned stages ran from anode and cathode electrode processing through unitized electrode assembly, stacking, compression, testing, and final assembly. The stated purpose was workforce talent and manufacturing process development for large-scale fuel cell commercialization, a goal the termination left unmet.
doe-osti-3031227-virtual-inspection-of-a:
Brian Giera of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory sums up a strategic project in abbreviated report LLNL-TR-2017038, dated April 2026. Checking and certifying 3D-printed parts for nuclear security work takes far more time and money than printing them. Hand review and X-ray scans are slow, and they link poorly to how a part was made. The project built a digital twin route: a software copy of the printing process that predicts the finished part.

Live process monitors feed the twin, so inspectors can judge a part virtually before cutting or scanning it. The aim is faster clearance with stronger proof for stockpile modernization work. Papers from the team cover a data framework for additive manufacturing built on FAIR principles, and a twin that tunes exposure times for structured light scanning gear.
doe-osti-3673458-multi-component-cavity-:
Aaron S. Rury of Wayne State University led the final report for award DE-SC0022134, submitted June 30, 2026. The performance period ran from August 2021 to December 2025. Team members came from Wayne State, the University of California campuses at Irvine and San Diego, Argonne, and Los Alamos. The subject is cavity polaritons, hybrid states that form when light is trapped near molecules and couples strongly to their electrons.

Four aims structure the work. The first built wider definitions of multipartite entanglement using algebra. The second sought light-based measures whose changes carry news of entanglement. The third made multi-cavity and multi-dye samples fit to create and test light-matter links. The fourth traced how excitation spreads between molecules in light-absorbing macromolecules. One study loaded paired zinc and copper porphyrin rings into plastic films inside cavities. Weak coupling should split their bright and dark states.
experiments-in-government-and-the-essent:
Root's Experiments in Government and the Essentials of the Constitution defends core constitutional limits. Elihu Root delivered the argument in 1913. He opens by naming two assaults then under way among civilized nations. One is socialism's attack on individualism, and the other targets existing institutions.

Root speaks to the second assault in the American setting. He assumes that liberty and private property must be maintained. Both, he says, underlie modern civilization itself. He contrasts the America of 1787 with his own day. States once lived apart behind slow communication barriers. Now production and commerce ignore state lines, he observes. The lectures weigh reform pressure against the Constitution's essentials.
jacobean-embroidery-its-forms-and-fillin:
Ada Wentworth Fitzwilliam and A. F. Morris Hands wrote Jacobean Embroidery, printed in London in 1912. Morris Hands supplies an introductory history, and plates show Tudor and seventeenth-century work. Some plates first ran in Needlecraft Monthly Magazine, the publishers note. Bed hangings at Hardwick Hall and Powis Castle are studied.

A faded strip from a bed valance is measured at five feet eight inches in one plate note. Its leaves run twenty-two inches long, in dark indigo blue and bright green wool. Blue leaves from old cushions at Knole Park follow. Fillings, stem stitch, and foliation are the book's craft.
love-life-work-being-a-book-of-opinions-:
Love, Life and Work is a book of opinions by Elbert Hubbard, dated 1906. Its subtitle promises good-natured views on reaching happiness with little harm to others. The chapters run from a prayer to essays on time, chance, and mental attitude. Hubbard writes on initiative, sympathy, knowledge, and poise.

He scolds the folly of living always in the future. He urges readers to get out or get in line, and to keep the weekday holy. His style is brisk, plain, and full of country common sense. Hubbard ran the Roycroft shops and spoke to plain working people. These short chapters still read like a friendly talk on living well.
nasa-tm-19630010327-lunar-flight-study-s:
B. J. Lisle of Marshall Space Flight Center wrote this study in April 1963. It is volume six of the Lunar Flight Study Series. The topic is trips between Earth and Moon that stay in one plane. Such flat paths are called coplanar transits in the report.

Lisle's abstract says the work maps the geometry of those transits. It links path behavior to changes in launch conditions, called injection. Start and end traits of each path get close attention. Planners of Moon flights needed such maps to pick safe routes. The study was bookkeeping for Apollo's age: which paths work, and how small errors bend them.
nasa-tm-19670022816-effect-of-wing-pivot:
William P. Henderson and Edward J. Ray, of NASA's Langley Research Center in Virginia, studied a swing-wing design in this investigation. The wing could sweep back and forth on a pivot, and it had an M-shaped planform. The question was where to put the pivot, because pivot position changes how the airplane balances.

Tests ran in Langley's high-speed tunnel, with and without tails and engine packs. Moving the pivot outboard, the results show, made an unstable break in the pitching behavior appear sooner. That break also grew generally more severe. The study gave designers a clearer picture of the trade-offs in pivot placement.
nasa-tm-19690008486-fortran-programs-for:
Harry H. Heyson of Langley Research Center presents Fortran programs for wind tunnel boundary interference in this report. Tunnel walls distort the airflow around a model, and interference factors correct the data. The programs here come from an earlier NASA report, TR R-302, and are printed without comment.

Heyson warns readers to study the earlier report's assumptions before using the code. The method computes interference for arbitrary configurations from calculations for a vanishingly small model. Swapping one subroutine adapts the code to a different tunnel. The underlying theory suits models with large wake deflections, such as V/STOL models. Conventional testing at moderate lift can also use the programs with small changes.
nasa-tm-19710009490-observations-of-acti:
Ronald Greeley of the Ames Research Center studied lava tubes while they were still forming in Hawaii. His report describes fluid basalt flows in the Upper East Rift Zone of Kilauea Volcano. In August 1970, lava poured from a vent near Alae Crater. It crossed the Chain of Craters Road inside Hawaii Volcanoes National Park.

Greeley watched the flows and compared them with older written accounts. From that evidence he reasoned about how lava tubes and channels develop. The tubes formed only in pahoehoe, the smooth, fluid kind of basalt flow. The report gives geologists a rare look at tube building caught in the act, not long after it cooled.
nasa-tm-19710018221-shock-and-vibration-:
Andre J Stromquist and Lawrence Hibben of the Lewis Research Center, with Robert S Foley of Aerojet General, reported these tests in May 1971. Their subject was the turboalternator of the SNAP-8 space power system. The machine joined a mercury vapor turbine to a generator. It had to survive the shaking and shocks of launch.

The unit took shock and vibration loads set by the SNAP-8 specification. Staff at Lewis and Aerojet then took the machine apart. Inspection found wear called galling that had shifted the turbine rotor slightly. Movement of the outer bearing rings was also restricted. Some outside plumbing and instruments had failed. Even so, the unit still operated and held its bearing preload.
nasa-tm-19720013274-engine-investigation:
Robert P Dengler, Frederick C Yeh, James W Gauntner, and Gerald E Fallon of the Lewis Research Center ran this blade test in a real engine. Their report came out in April 1972, as NASA TM X-2526. The test blade was a turbine rotor blade cooled by air. Jets struck its leading edge from inside. Lengthwise passages carried air along the chord. A slotted rear edge let the air escape. Most cooling data then came from still laboratory rigs.

The engine ran with inlet gas heat between two thousand and twenty five hundred degrees Fahrenheit. Gas pressure also spanned a working range. The team presents the measured metal temperatures from those runs. Both average and local heat transfer results are included. Engine truth helped check the cheaper cascade methods.
podcast-dannyjones-Y0KsiUg8UtU:
Writer Jordan Rubin takes Danny Jones inside America's shadow war on clandestine chemistry. Rubin has reported on underground drug labs and the people who run them. The episode covers the hidden front of the drug war, where home chemists and federal agents chase each other.

Rubin explains how secret labs make drugs that laws have not yet named. He describes raids, fires, and the cat-and-mouse game over precursor chemicals. Jones asks who these chemists are and what drives them to risk prison. Curious and wary listeners get a rare look at labs in the dark and busts in the light.
podcast-dannyjones-th0tVVOvltU:
Investigative reporter Sean Naylor joins Danny Jones to discuss covert war. Naylor works with fellow reporter Jack Murphy on the Highside project. Their outlet covers secret units and hidden campaigns.

Naylor warns that the CIA is training a new class of global killers. He bases the claim on years of reporting on special operations. Jones asks how such programs stay hidden from the public. The episode gives a reporter's case, drawn from sources and records, about a shadow war that voters rarely get to debate. The claims are grave, and he states them plainly.
poets-of-the-south-a-series-of-biographi:
F. V. N. Painter, professor of modern languages at Roanoke College, wrote Poets of the South to correct a neglect: the South's singers, he argues, are little read even in the South. His book offers biographical and critical studies with typical poems, annotated, so that readers meet each poet through both a life and a selection. Painter blames an age of prose and practical interests for the drift away from poetic truth.

Five leaders receive chief consideration: Poe, Hayne, Timrod, Lanier, and Ryan, the chorus masters of southern verse, though minor poets and their gems are not forgotten. Painter wrote during a southern literary renaissance, when the region was reading more and reclaiming its older authors. His studies are generous, sometimes defensive, and wholly earnest. An educator's brief for the claim that the South's poets deserve a higher place in American letters than they had been given.
the-ancient-church-its-history-doctrine-:
W. D. Killen, professor of church history and pastoral work for the Presbyterian Church in Ireland, traces the ancient church through its first three hundred years. His title promises four threads: its history, its teaching, its worship, and its frame of rule. The New York edition is dated 1859 in Roman numerals.

In a note at the front, Killen thanks Charles Scribner of New York, the first publisher in the old world or the new to urge him on in the task. Scribner's prompt and kind offers, he says, helped fix plans for the book in Great Britain. Every line of this printing was corrected by Killen himself.
the-white-ladies-of-worcester-a-romance-: Florence L. Barclay, author of The Rosary and The Mistress of Shenstone, published The White Ladies of Worcester as a romance of the twelfth century ghosts. Harry E. Townsend drew its endpapers and ground-plan. The pages present here hold the front matter and a partial contents list, so the romance itself does not appear. Early chapters visit a pilgrim at the gospels and find the Bishop of Sauvenac at the shrine of Saint Cuthberga. Later headings promise a bishop's dream, a noble company, and a mighty host.
